schools.summary: Gill takes nabal for a whole class of wicked, profane men (not idiots), who say 'no God' in the heart; Calvin makes it not the common dullard but the perverse and wise-in-their-own-eyes, since no stupidity is more brutish than forgetting God, and the licence of their life, not any argument, sings them the atheist's song.
Clarke sorts the atheism into three sorts (deny existence, deny providence, deny in heart and life); Wesley glosses 'fool' as the wicked man and 'good' as actions truly pleasing to God.

Henry hears the creed whispered secretly, wished true though unproven, said only when it is the sinner's interest that none call him to account; Spurgeon calls the atheist the fool pre-eminent, belying the plainest evidence and stifling conscience.

Ellicott derives nabal from a root 'to wither,' fool and wicked near-synonymous, noting the twin reads 'iniquity' for 'works'; Keil and Delitzsch mark Psalm 53 as the Elohimic recurrence and this Jehovic form as the earlier, more original.
Augustine reads the title's 'end' toward Christ, to whom the believer presses.

outliers.note: Reads the superscription typologically — the 'end' of the title taken for Christ, the goal to which the believer presses — rather than as a musical direction.

themes: the fool hath said in his heart

schools.summary: Gill reads the looking-down as a direct rejoinder to the atheist's reasonings — an anthropopathy, spoken after the manner of men, yet consistent with God's omniscience and omnipresence.

Keil and Delitzsch: the verb means to bend forward and look as from a window, 'to see' recalling the tower of Babel (Gen. 11:5); Ellicott renders 'bent forward to look as from a window' and prefers 'any man of understanding,' set against the 'fool.'

Clarke pictures God from his eminence looking to see if any understand a Supreme Being and seek him; Wesley: God knows all without enquiry, the 'children of men' the nation and all mankind, his people excepted.
Spurgeon dwells on the justice of the search (God visited Sodom before overthrowing it), yet owns it fruitless — no unrenewed soul but is an enemy to God.

themes: the LORD looked down from heaven
anthropomorphism after the manner of men
any that understand and seek God

schools.summary: Gill hears the men gone aside as bankrupts run out of their stock, revolted from God; Paul renders it 'gone out of the way,' out of righteousness into sin and death.
Henry (whose comment reaches from v.1) calls the apostasy universal — none doeth good till grace works the change — all good in men being God's work in them.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh hakol/yachdav/none-excepted, sar as apostasy and ne'elach as putrefaction (Job 15:16), and note Paul quotes vv.1-3 (Rom. 3:10-12) to shut Jew and heathen under sin; Ellicott glosses 'filthy' as corrupt/putrid (with Juvenal) and traces the interpolation.

Clarke draws the dairy image — sour and rancid like fermented milk, the state of all until grace — and reports the six added verses (Rom. 3:13-18); Wesley reads them gone from God, 'filthy' as loathsome and abominable.
Augustine finds in 'up to one' room for the Lord Christ to be excepted, since none did good until he first showed it.

debates.question: Do the six verses the ancient versions add after v.3 (Rom. 3:13-18) belong to the psalm, or are they an interpolation?

sides.position: an interpolation — a cento Paul gathered from various psalms and Isaiah, later copied into the Greek psalter from Romans
original to the psalm — Paul quoted the six verses from the text as it then stood, later lost from most copies

outliers.note: Reads 'there is none that doeth good, no, not one' as leaving Christ excepted — none did good 'up to' (short of) the one Christ, who first showed goodness.

schools.summary: Gill reads 'no knowledge?' as marvelling or denying — not sinners of the Gentiles but sinners in Zion, who had the revelation and law and so sinned against knowledge.

Keil and Delitzsch take 'not to know' absolutely, as without sense or conscience, aimed at Israel's sinners (Isa. 3:13-15); Ellicott fixes the Hebrew 'eating my people they have eaten bread,' a proverbial saying (Mic. 3:3-4), and Homer's 'people-devouring kings.'
Henry hears inveterate enmity — they devour God's people as bread, like Joseph's brethren; Spurgeon heaps figures (pikes, eagles, wolves) and notes that preying they forswear praying.
Clarke makes them an easy prey, the saints 'bread for us' (Num. 14:9), and 'call not' marking them atheists or idolaters; Wesley: eaten with greediness, guilty of injustice to men and impiety to God.

themes: eat up my people as bread

schools.summary: Gill takes the fear as proof of a guilty conscience the atheist cannot banish (the wicked flee when none pursues; Hobbes afraid in the dark), and notes the twin adds 'where no fear was.'

Keil and Delitzsch read 'there' as 'then' — when God's word smites them — the doubled 'feared a fear' heaping intensity; Ellicott finds in the local 'there' a picture, warns it fixes no particular event, and notes the twin's added 'which was no fear.'
Clarke sees an allusion to the Canaanites' terror at Israel and the versions' 'where no fear was'; Wesley: God struck them with panic on the spot, being on his people's side.
Spurgeon: as cowards are cruel, cruel men are cowards; the persecutors quail because they perceive God is with his people — like Haman before Mordecai.

themes: there were they in great fear
God in the generation of the righteous

schools.summary: Gill makes the poor the saints and the 'counsel' the counsel they receive from the Lord — to make him their refuge — which the wicked deride, though hope makes not ashamed.

Keil and Delitzsch: the verb with a thing-object means to confound or frustrate the counsel, the psalmist meeting the oppressed with joyous confidence (a distich for the expected tristich); Ellicott takes 'counsel' as the sufferer's confidence and reads a present challenge, faulting the AV's past tense.

Clarke rejects Horsley's proposed repointing and keeps the past — the poor took counsel to wait on God, which the proud derided; Wesley: the ground of contempt was that the poor lived by faith in God's promise.
Spurgeon: the wicked put on the lion's skin and mock the believer's confidence ('What can your God do for you now?'), but let us not be laughed out of our refuge.

debates.question: Is the verb a past accusation ('ye have shamed') or a present taunt ('would ye make the sufferer blush?')?

sides.position: a present challenge met at once by faith — the AV wrongly used the past tense
a past accusation of shame already attempted — the received reading

themes: shamed the counsel of the poor

schools.summary: Gill hears the Messiah in 'salvation' — the Saviour out of Zion, out of Judea — David longing, amid the depravity described, for that coming.

Keil and Delitzsch gloss 'bring back the captivity' (shuv shevut), redemption looked for only from Zion, and hear the closing tristich as perhaps an exilic liturgical addition; Ellicott has the exiles turning to the Holy City (as Daniel prayed), 'turn the captivity' proverbial for any misfortune (Job 42:10).

Clarke judges the whole psalm a complaint of the Babylonian captives, the ascription to David wrongly prefixed (Calmet on Israel and Judah rejoined); Wesley: the immediate deliverance, but principally the Messiah's spiritual redemption of all God's Israel.

Henry keeps it David's own (the flight from Absalom) yet lets it look to the Redeemer coming to Zion (Rom. 11:26) and the second coming; Spurgeon makes it the desire of the godly in all ages, still looking for Christ's second advent unto salvation.

debates.question: What is the psalm's occasion — David's own day or the Babylonian exile?

sides.position: David's own time — the flight from Absalom
the Babylonian captivity — the ascription to David wrongly prefixed
a Davidic psalm whose closing verse may be an exilic liturgical addition
